title: Crashes and the Fight for Safety
summary: Cars gave people amazing freedom, but they also brought a new danger: crashes. Clever inventors fought back with windscreen wipers, safety glass, seatbelts, crumple zones and airbags. Thanks to them, a ride in a car today is far safer than it was for your grandparents, though there is still work to do.

sections.heading: A Scientist on a Steam Carriage
paragraphs: Our story starts not on a busy city street but on a quiet country road in Ireland, beside a castle with a giant telescope. The town was called Parsonstown at the time; today it is Birr, in County Offaly. In the grounds of Birr Castle stood the Leviathan, for decades the largest telescope in the world, built by William Parsons, the third Earl of Rosse.

The Earl's cousin, Mary Ward, was a remarkable scientist. Born Mary King in 1827, she had been collecting insects since she was about three years old. She taught herself to use a microscope, made her own glass slides from thin slices of ivory, and drew what she saw with beautiful precision. Her book Sketches with the Microscope, first printed privately in 1857 in just 250 copies, proved so popular that it was later published for everyone and reprinted again and again. She also wrote a book about telescopes and was one of only three women on the mailing list of the Royal Astronomical Society, at a time when women were barred from most universities and scientific societies.

The Parsons family loved machines. The Earl's sons, who included the young Charles Parsons, later famous for inventing the steam turbine, had built a small steam-powered road carriage. On 31 August 1869, Mary Ward was riding on it with family members along the road near the town. As it went round a bend, the carriage lurched, and she was thrown off and fell under one of its heavy iron wheels. She died almost at once. She was 42.

Mary Ward's death is often called the first known death caused by a motor vehicle. Historians add a careful note, though: steam carriages had caused accidents before. In 1834 a steam carriage boiler exploded in Scotland, near Paisley, and several passengers were killed. So it is fairer to say that Mary Ward is the first person widely recorded as being killed by a self-propelled road vehicle, and that her death was an early sign of what powerful machines on roads could do. Her microscope and books can still be seen in Ireland today.

Notice something important about this first tragedy. Nobody was being careless on purpose. The vehicle simply had no seatbelts, no doors and nothing to hold a passenger in place, and nobody had yet thought about what happens to a human body when a heavy machine stops or swerves suddenly. Working that out would take another century.

sections.heading: Crystal Palace, 1896: A Car Meets a Pedestrian
paragraphs: Twenty-seven years later, in the summer of 1896, petrol cars were brand new in Britain. Parliament was about to change the law to let them travel at up to 14 mph, as you read in Part 2, though the new rules would not start until that November. Crowds gathered at the Crystal Palace, a gigantic glass-and-iron exhibition building in south London, where a company called the Anglo-French Motor Carriage Company was giving people demonstration rides in its cars.

On 17 August 1896, a 44-year-old woman named Bridget Driscoll was crossing a terrace in the Crystal Palace grounds with her teenage daughter and a friend. A demonstration car driven by a young man named Arthur Edsall came towards them. Witnesses said she seemed confused about which way to step, as many people would have been when faced with a machine they had never seen before. The car struck her, and she died within minutes from a head injury.

At the inquest, the official inquiry into her death, people disagreed about how fast the car had been going. One witness described it as moving at 'a reckless pace, in fact, like a fire engine'. The driver said he was going only about 4 mph, the speed the car had been set to, and a cab driver who examined the car said it could not go faster than about 4.5 mph. After about six hours, the jury decided it was an accidental death. The coroner, Percy Morrison, said he hoped that 'such a thing would never happen again'.

Bridget Driscoll is remembered as the first pedestrian in Britain to be killed by a petrol car. The coroner's hope, sadly, was not fulfilled. As millions of cars filled the roads in the following decades, crashes became common. In many countries, more people were killed on the roads each year than by most diseases. Something had to be done, but at first people blamed drivers, not machines. The idea that cars themselves could be designed to protect people grew only slowly.

sections.heading: Seeing Clearly: Wipers, Safety Glass and Headlights
paragraphs: Some of the earliest safety inventions were about something very simple: being able to see. On a snowy day in New York City, around 1902, an Alabama woman named Mary Anderson rode on a streetcar, a kind of electric tram. She noticed that the driver kept having to open his window or lean out to wipe snow and sleet off the glass with his hand, letting cold air blow in on the passengers. There had to be a better way.

Back home, she designed a device with a rubber blade on the outside of the windscreen, connected to a lever inside. By swinging the lever, the driver could sweep the blade back and forth across the glass without ever opening the window. A counterweight kept the blade pressed against the glass, and the whole thing could be taken off when winter was over. On 10 November 1903 she was granted US Patent number 743,801 for a 'window cleaning device'.

Anderson tried to sell her idea to companies, but they said it had no commercial value. Her patent lasted 17 years and ran out in 1920 without making her any money. Yet hand-operated wipers became normal on cars in the following years, and in 1917 another American woman, Charlotte Bridgwood, patented an electric 'storm windshield cleaner', an early automatic wiper. In 2011 Mary Anderson was added to the US National Inventors Hall of Fame.

Another danger lurked in the windscreen itself. Ordinary glass breaks into long, sharp, dagger-like shards. In a crash, people were badly cut by flying glass. According to a well-known story, around 1903 the French chemist Édouard Bénédictus knocked a glass flask off a shelf in his laboratory and was surprised to see that it cracked but stayed in one piece. The flask had held a plastic solution called cellulose nitrate, which had dried into a thin film on the inside and held the broken glass together. Whether or not every detail of the story is true, Bénédictus did go on to patent laminated safety glass, made of a sandwich of glass and a clear plastic layer, in 1909.

Laminated glass was used for gas-mask eyepieces during the First World War and gradually found its way into cars. By the late 1920s Ford was fitting safety-glass windscreens to its Model A. Today car windscreens are made of laminated glass, so that when a stone hits them they crack like a spider's web but do not shatter into the car. Side windows are usually toughened glass, which breaks into small, blunt pebbles instead of sharp blades.

Seeing at night was another problem. The first cars used candle or oil lamps and then acetylene gas lamps, which made a bright flame but had to be lit by hand and refilled. In 1912 Cadillac offered a complete electric system, with Charles Kettering's self-starter (Part 7), a generator, a battery and electric lights. Electric headlights could be switched on with a flick, and later designs added dipped beams so drivers would not dazzle people coming the other way. Brake lights, indicators and reflectors followed, all helping drivers see and be seen.

sections.heading: Béla Barényi and the Car That Crumples on Purpose
paragraphs: For a long time, many people believed that the strongest, stiffest car was the safest. If a car came out of a crash with hardly a dent, surely that was good? An engineer named Béla Barényi realised this was exactly wrong.

Barényi was born on 1 March 1907 in Hirtenberg, a small town in Austria, then part of Austria-Hungary. As a student in Vienna he was already sketching ideas for safer, cleverer cars. After working for several car companies, he joined Daimler-Benz in Germany in 1939, and he spent the rest of his career there, heading a department that worked on future designs until he retired in 1972.

Here is the key idea. When a car hits a wall, it stops suddenly. The people inside keep moving forward until something stops them too. What hurts people is not speed itself but stopping too quickly, because the faster you stop, the bigger the force on your body. Think of catching a raw egg. If you hold your hands stiff, the egg smashes. If you let your hands move back as you catch it, the egg slows down gradually and survives.

Barényi's answer was to divide the car into zones. The front and rear would be crumple zones, designed to fold up in a controlled way during a crash, like a can being squashed. As the metal crumples, it soaks up the energy of the crash and stretches out the time it takes for the car to stop, by a tiny fraction of a second, which makes a huge difference to the people inside. In the middle, around the passengers, he wanted a strong, rigid passenger cell, a safety cage that would not collapse onto the people inside.

Barényi had worked on the idea since the 1930s, and in 1952 he received a German patent (number 854157) for the design. In 1959 Mercedes-Benz launched a new family of saloon cars, nicknamed the 'Fintail' because of the small fins on the rear, which was the first car built fully around his crumple-zone design. The same year, Mercedes-Benz began crashing real cars into obstacles to test them, a practice that has become standard across the industry.

Barényi had many other safety ideas, including steering columns that collapse instead of spearing into the driver's chest, and stronger roof pillars to protect people if a car rolls over. He is often called the father of passive safety, which means safety features that protect you automatically without you having to do anything. Patent experts count well over a thousand patents filed in his name around the world. Every modern car is designed to crumple at the ends and stay strong in the middle, just as he imagined.

sections.heading: Nils Bohlin's Belt: Three Points That Saved Millions
paragraphs: A crumple zone slows the car gently, but it only helps if you slow down with the car. Without a belt, a person in a crash keeps flying forward and hits the steering wheel, dashboard or windscreen, or is thrown out of the car altogether. Seatbelts hold you in place so that you share the car's gentler stop.

Belts themselves were not new. Aircraft had used them for years, and some early cars had them. In 1949 the American company Nash offered lap belts, which go across the hips, in its cars, but few buyers wanted them. Saab in Sweden fitted belts as standard in 1958. But lap belts and diagonal belts had problems. A lap belt alone lets the upper body fold forward violently. A belt across only the chest can let a person slide out underneath it.

In 1958 Volvo, the Swedish carmaker, hired a safety engineer named Nils Bohlin. Bohlin had spent years at the aircraft company Saab designing ejection seats, which fire pilots out of a damaged fighter jet. He knew a lot about what happens to a human body under huge forces. In about a year he designed the three-point seatbelt: one strap goes across the lap and another diagonally across the chest, joined at a single buckle beside the hip, and anchored low so it stays in place during a crash. The straps rest over the strong bones of the hips and the chest, spreading the force. It could be put on with one hand in a couple of seconds.

The first car sold with Bohlin's three-point belts was a Volvo PV544, delivered in Sweden in August 1959. Then Volvo did something unusual. Instead of keeping the design to itself, it made the patent available for other carmakers to use free of charge, because the company believed the belt was too important for safety to be kept secret. Today the three-point belt is fitted to practically every car in the world.

Bohlin also collected evidence. In 1967 he presented a study of about 28,000 crashes in Sweden. It found that, in crashes below about 60 mph where the passenger compartment stayed in one piece, no one wearing a belt had been killed. Studies since then show that wearing a seatbelt cuts the risk of death for people in the front seats by roughly half. Volvo estimates that the three-point belt has saved more than a million lives worldwide.

Of course, a belt only works if it is worn, and for years many people did not bother. Laws helped. In 1970 the state of Victoria in Australia became the first place in the world to require drivers and front-seat passengers to wear belts. Many other countries followed: the United Kingdom made belts compulsory for front-seat occupants in 1983, and in 1984 New York became the first US state with a seatbelt law. Campaigns such as 'Clunk Click Every Trip' in Britain helped make buckling up a habit.

sections.heading: Unsafe at Any Speed: Laws, Rules and Dummies
paragraphs: In the United States in the 1960s, around 50,000 people were dying on the roads every year. Many carmakers spent large sums changing the style of their cars each year, with new fins, chrome and colours, but much less on making them safer. The common view was that crashes were caused by 'the nut behind the wheel', meaning bad drivers, so the car itself was not to blame.

A young lawyer named Ralph Nader disagreed. In November 1965 he published a book called Unsafe at Any Speed. It argued that cars were designed with too little thought for what happens in a crash: hard dashboards, sharp knobs, steering columns that could push into a driver's chest, and confusing controls. Its best-known chapter criticised the handling of the early Chevrolet Corvair. (Later government tests disputed some of the claims about the Corvair, and historians still argue about it, but the book's wider point about safety design was very influential.)

The book became a bestseller, and things got even more dramatic when it came out that General Motors had hired private investigators to follow Nader and look for embarrassing information about him. In March 1966 the president of General Motors apologised to Nader in front of a US Senate committee. Nader later sued the company for invading his privacy and won a settlement, which he used to help fund car-safety campaigns.

The public outcry helped Congress act. On 9 September 1966, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act, which for the first time let the US government set compulsory safety standards for new cars. Soon new cars had to have seatbelts, padded dashboards, energy-absorbing steering columns, shatter-resistant windscreens and dual braking systems. In 1970 a new government agency, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, or NHTSA, was set up to write and enforce these rules and investigate crashes.

To test whether cars really protected people, engineers needed something to put inside them during crashes. Early researchers sometimes used volunteers in carefully controlled experiments. The US Air Force doctor John Paul Stapp famously rode rocket sleds that braked from over 1,000 km/h in less than a couple of seconds, to learn how much force a human body can survive. Obviously, real people could not be used in full car crashes, so engineers built crash-test dummies.

One of the first, named Sierra Sam, was built in 1949 to test aircraft ejection seats. In 1976 a dummy called Hybrid III appeared, and versions of it are still used today. A modern dummy is packed with sensors in its head, neck, chest and legs, recording tens of thousands of measurements in the tenth of a second a crash lasts. Dummies now come in families: different sizes of adults, children and, more recently, dummies designed to represent women's bodies more accurately, because for many years most dummies were modelled on an average man. Organisations such as Euro NCAP, founded in 1997, crash-test new cars and give them star ratings, so buyers can compare safety.

sections.heading: Airbags, Smart Brakes and Child Seats
paragraphs: A seatbelt holds your body, but in a hard crash your head can still swing forward. The airbag is a cushion that inflates in front of you faster than you can blink. An American engineer named John Hetrick patented a car airbag in 1953, after his family car swerved into a ditch. Early designs used compressed air, which turned out to be too slow. The breakthrough came in the late 1960s with an electronic crash sensor and a small chemical charge that produces a burst of gas, mostly nitrogen, filling the bag in about 20 to 30 thousandths of a second.

General Motors offered airbags on some cars in the 1970s, including the 1973 Oldsmobile Toronado, but few buyers chose them. In 1981 Mercedes-Benz offered a driver's airbag on its S-Class, designed to work together with the seatbelt. From the late 1980s and through the 1990s airbags spread quickly, and in the United States every new car built from the 1998 model year had to have front airbags for both the driver and front passenger. Side airbags and curtain airbags, which protect the head in side impacts, arrived in the 1990s. Airbags are designed to work with seatbelts, not instead of them. They are also the reason small children should not sit in a front seat with an active airbag.

Another danger was skidding. If you slam on the brakes hard, the wheels can lock and stop turning, and a car sliding on locked wheels cannot be steered. Aircraft had used anti-skid systems for years. In 1978 the German company Bosch, working with Mercedes-Benz, introduced an electronic anti-lock braking system, or ABS, on the S-Class. Sensors watch each wheel, and if one is about to lock, a computer briefly releases and reapplies the brake many times a second. The driver feels the pedal pulsing, and, most importantly, can still steer around an obstacle while braking hard.

In 1995 Bosch and Mercedes-Benz took the idea further with electronic stability control, or ESC. If sensors detect that the car is starting to skid sideways or spin, the system gently brakes individual wheels to bring the car back into line. Studies found it greatly reduces crashes in which cars slide off the road, and from the early 2010s it became compulsory on new cars in the United States and the European Union.

Children need special protection because their bodies are smaller and their neck and bones are still developing. In 1964 the Swedish professor Bertil Aldman, inspired by the way astronauts lay on their backs facing backwards during launch, developed an early rear-facing child seat that Volvo tested. A rear-facing seat spreads the crash forces across a baby's whole back and head instead of throwing the head forward. According to the World Health Organization, using proper child restraints can cut deaths among infants in crashes by about 71 percent.

Safety is not only about machines. Drinking alcohol before driving makes crashes far more likely. In 1954 the American scientist Robert Borkenstein invented the Breathalyzer, a device that measures alcohol in a person's breath, making drink-driving laws much easier to enforce. In 1980 Candace Lightner, whose 13-year-old daughter had been killed by a drunk driver, founded Mothers Against Drunk Driving in California, and campaigns like it changed public attitudes in many countries. Lower speed limits near schools, speed cameras, helmets for motorcyclists and cyclists, and better road designs such as roundabouts and safe crossings have all helped too.

sections.heading: How Safe Are We Now?
paragraphs: So, has all this worked? In many countries, the answer is a strong yes. In the United States in the mid-1960s, about five people died for every 100 million miles driven. In recent years the figure has been around 1.3, even though Americans now drive several times more miles in total. In Great Britain, almost 8,000 people died on the roads in 1966; in recent years the number has been around 1,600, despite far more traffic. Seatbelts, crumple zones, airbags, ABS, better roads, better emergency medicine and tougher laws all played a part.

But the world as a whole still has a very serious problem. The World Health Organization's 2023 global report estimated that about 1.19 million people die in road crashes every year, and its latest fact sheet gives a similar figure of about 1.16 million. That is roughly one person every half-minute. Between 20 and 50 million more are injured. Road injuries are the leading cause of death for children and young people aged 5 to 29 worldwide.

The danger is not shared equally. According to the WHO, about 92 percent of road deaths happen in low- and middle-income countries, even though those countries have only around 60 percent of the world's vehicles. More than half of the people killed are not inside cars at all: they are pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists, the people with the least protection, just like Bridget Driscoll in 1896.

The United Nations has set a goal of halving road deaths and injuries by 2030. Experts talk about a 'safe system' approach: accepting that people will always make mistakes, and designing cars, roads, speeds and rules so that those mistakes do not cost lives. Sweden's 'Vision Zero' policy, adopted in 1997, aims for a future where nobody is killed or seriously injured on the roads at all.

Today engineers are working on cars that can brake automatically if they sense a pedestrian, warn drivers who drift out of their lane, and protect people outside the car with softer bonnets and even pedestrian airbags. Yet while the fight against crashes was going on, another, quieter danger was building up. It could not be seen in a crash test, and no seatbelt could protect anyone from it. It was coming out of the tailpipe.

deepDive: The physics of car safety comes down to one idea: what injures people is not speed but sudden changes in speed. The force on a body depends on how quickly it decelerates. A person moving at 50 km/h who stops in one-hundredth of a second experiences a force roughly ten times greater than if the same stop is stretched over a tenth of a second. Crumple zones, seatbelts that stretch slightly, belt pretensioners and load limiters, and airbags that vent gas as you sink into them are all ways of lengthening that stopping time and spreading the force over the strongest parts of the body. Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, which is why speed limits matter so much: a crash at 60 km/h carries about 44 percent more energy than one at 50 km/h. The WHO estimates that each 1 percent rise in average speed increases the risk of a fatal crash by about 4 percent, and a pedestrian hit at around 30 km/h is far more likely to survive than one hit at 50 km/h. Historians and safety researchers also debate why road deaths fell. Engineering improvements are one part. Others include seatbelt laws, drink-driving enforcement, better trauma care and ambulances, divided motorways, and more cautious driving cultures. Some economists, notably Sam Peltzman in the 1970s, argued that safety features might encourage riskier driving and cancel out some benefits, an idea called risk compensation. Later studies generally found that safety features still saved many lives overall, though the effect is not always as large as engineers expected. Another debate is about fairness: crash-test dummies were long based on an average man, and some studies suggest women have faced higher injury risks in comparable crashes, which is why new female dummies are being developed. Finally, the claims of firsts need care. Mary Ward is often called the first motor-vehicle fatality, but earlier steam-carriage accidents, such as the 1834 boiler explosion near Paisley in Scotland, killed passengers. Volvo's 'more than a million lives saved' is the company's own estimate, but independent studies agree that seatbelts are among the most effective safety devices ever invented.
funFact: When Volvo introduced Nils Bohlin's three-point seatbelt in 1959, it let other carmakers use the patent for free, so a single design ended up protecting drivers of almost every brand of car in the world.

check.q: What does a crumple zone do in a crash?
check.a: It crushes in a controlled way to absorb energy and slow the car more gently, protecting the people inside
wrong: It makes the car bounce back off whatever it hits
It pumps air into the tyres so the car stops faster
It locks the doors so nobody can get out
